t: Find the error: "He was killed with a terrorist."
e: A living doer in passive voice takes 'by' → "killed by a terrorist".

t: Fill in the blank: His behaviour is ______ control now.
e: 'Beyond control/doubt/repair' is fixed.

t: Fill in the blank: He walked ______ the tunnel to reach the other side.
e: 'Through' is used for passing inside something like a tunnel.

t: Find the error: "He is married with a doctor."
e: Active voice 'married' never takes a preposition → "He is married to a doctor" (passive 'to' only).

t: Find the error: "Despite of facing a lot of criticism, he continued his work."
o: Despite of facing a lot of criticism
e: 'Despite' never takes 'of' → "Despite facing a lot of criticism".

t: Fill in the blank: Please compare your answer ______ mine; they're very similar.
e: 'Compare with' is used for similar things.

t: Find the error: "We discussed about the project yesterday."
e: 'Discuss' never takes 'about' → "discussed the project".

t: Fill in the blank: My success ______ this project depends ______ your support.
e: 'Depend on/upon' is fixed; 'success in' a project is standard usage.

t: Find the error: "She is capable to handle this project."
e: 'Capable' takes 'of' + gerund → "capable of handling".

t: Find the error: "He proposed his parents that they should travel abroad."
e: 'Propose' takes 'to' before a human indirect object → "proposed to his parents".

t: Fill in the blank: I have known her ______ 2010.
e: 'Since' is used with a fixed point of time (2010); 'for' is used with duration.

t: Find the error: "She was born on 1998."
e: Years take 'in' → "born in 1998".

t: Find the error: "The meeting is scheduled at Monday."
e: Days take 'on' → "scheduled on Monday".

t: Fill in the blank: We must abstain ______ alcohol during treatment.
e: 'Abstain', 'refrain', 'prevent', 'differ' (in origin sense) take 'from'.

t: Fill in the blank: The suspect burst ______ tears during questioning.
e: 'Burst into tears/laughter' is a fixed phrase.

t: Find the error: "His house is farther from mine on this issue."
o: farther from mine on this issue
e: For abstract/figurative distance, 'further' is used, not 'farther' (physical distance) → "further on this issue" doesn't fit physically either; correct usage: "His argument goes further on this issue."

t: Find the error: "He is superior than his rival in every aspect."
e: Words ending in '-ior' (superior, senior, junior, prior) take 'to', never 'than' → "superior to his rival".

t: Find the error: "I am not aware about the new rules."
o: not aware about the new rules

t: Fill in the blank: He complained ______ the noisy neighbours to the police.
e: 'Complain against' is used for a person; 'complain about' is used for a thing.

t: Fill in the blank: ______ being talented, he is also very hardworking.
e: 'Besides' means 'in addition to'.

t: Find the error: "Ram is sitting besides Sita."
e: 'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means in addition to → "sitting beside Sita".

t: Find the error: "Your curry tastes different than the one we had yesterday."
e: 'Different' takes 'from', not 'than' → "different from the one".

t: Fill in the blank: He is currently ______ investigation for fraud.
e: 'Under investigation/pressure/consideration' is fixed.

t: Fill in the blank: We will meet you ______ tomorrow.
e: 'Tomorrow', 'today', 'yesterday' take no preposition.

t: Fill in the blank: He was surprised ______ her sudden visit.
e: 'Surprised', 'shocked', 'laugh', 'good/bad (at a skill)' take 'at'.

t: Find the error: "The garden was full with roses."
e: 'Full' takes 'of', not 'with' → "full of roses".

t: Fill in the blank: The two countries agreed to ______ into a treaty.
e: For joining an agreement/debate, 'enter into' is correct (exception to the 'Enter' rule).

t: Find the error: "He is very fond to eat spicy food."
e: 'Fond' takes 'of' + gerund → "fond of eating spicy food".

t: Fill in the blank: This gift is ______ you and me only.
e: 'Between' is used for exactly two people, paired with 'and'.

t: Find the error: "The match was stopped because the heavy rain."
e: 'Because' (conjunction) takes a clause; before a noun phrase use 'because of' → "because of the heavy rain".

t: Fill in the blank: She is engrossed ______ her studies these days.
e: 'Engrossed', 'absorbed', 'involved', 'interested' take 'in'.

t: Find the error: "My parents forbade to me from going out at night."
e: 'Forbade' never takes 'to' before the person → "forbade me from going out".

t: Fill in the blank: He is known ______ me for many years. (Voice/Preposition fixed list — known TO)
e: 'Known to' (not 'by') is the fixed passive-voice preposition.

t: Find the error: "This job requires someone to rely."
e: 'Rely' needs 'on' as its object preposition → "someone to rely on".

t: Find the error: "The show starts from 9 pm."
e: 'Start' does not take 'from' → "The show starts at 9 pm."

t: Find the error: "He is still coping up with his mother's death."
o: coping up with his mother's death
e: The correct phrase is 'cope with', not 'cope up with' → "coping with his mother's death".

t: Find the error: "The Prime Minister will preside over on the meeting."
e: 'Preside' takes only 'over', not 'over on' → "preside over the meeting".

t: Find the error: "You should dispose off all the extra items."

t: Find the error: "He had no one to talk."
o: He had no one to talk

t: Find the error: "The police are investigating into the murder case."
e: 'Investigate' never takes 'into' → "investigating the murder case".

t: Find the error: "She was accused for theft in the office."
e: 'Accused' takes 'of', not 'for' → "accused of theft".

t: Find the error: "Please revert back to me by tomorrow."
e: 'Re-' already means back; 'revert back' is redundant → "revert to me".

t: Find the error: "The ball rolled in the yard from the porch."
e: Motion into a place needs 'into', not the static 'in' → "rolled into the yard".

t: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of prepositions.

t: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of preposition.
o: What's the difference both cardiac arrest and a heart attack?
What's the difference by cardiac arrest and a heart attack?
What's the difference of cardiac arrest and a heart attack?
What's the difference between cardiac arrest and a heart attack?
e: The preposition 'between' is used to distinguish or talk about the relation between two things. Among the given options, only option (d) represents the sentence with the appropriate use of a preposition. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer. Note: A Preposition is a word placed before a noun or a pronoun or a noun equivalent (pronoun, adverb, gerund, infinitive, adverbial clause, or any clause that can be used as the object of the preposition) and shows a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between two or more people, places, or things in a sentence. t: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of preposition.
o: Opportunity never knocks twice by any man's door.
Opportunity never knocks twice in any man's door.

t:

t: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of preposition.
o: Are you interested along with modern art?
Are you interested into modern art?
Are you interested with modern art?

t: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of preposition.
o: When you are on Rome, do as Rome does.
When you are away Rome, do as Rome does.
When you are at Rome, do as Rome does.

t:

He rushed _______ the room with his coat on.
e: 'Into' means moving towards the inside of anything. The correct sentence is- He rushed into the room with his coat on. Hence, option (a) is correct.

t: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of preposition.
o: They've been best friends when they were children.
They've been best friends by they were children.
They've been best friends for they were children.
They've been best friends since they were children.
e:
The use of the present perfect tense indicates that the event/action started in the past and continues to the present. The sentence conveys that their friendship started when they were children. So, it is a point of time in the past. In this type of reference, 'since' is the correct choice. E.g., We have been married since 1997.
Hence, option (d) is the correct answer. 
By - We use 'by' meaning 'not later than' to refer to arrangements and deadlines.
For - used before a given period of time. 
When - used to refer to a future situation or condition that we are certain of.

t:
Select the appropriate preposition for the given blanks.
We have a meeting scheduled ______ Monday to discuss the new project.
e: On- Before the names of days and dates. The correct sentence is- We have a meeting scheduled on Monday to discuss the new project. Hence, option (b) is correct. In - expressing the situation of something that is or appears to be enclosed or surrounded by something else. By - used to refer to the doer of the action in the passive voice. She was admitted to his office immediately _____ her arrival.

Hence, option (c) is correct. To - to indicate a destination or direction. Among - situated more or less centrally in relation to (several other things). For - used to indicate the place someone or something is going to or toward. In - expressing the situation of something that is or appears to be enclosed or surrounded by something else.

t:
Select the appropriate preposition for the given blanks.
The treasure is buried _____ the well.
e:
The blank requires a preposition that denotes the location of the place in which the treasure is buried. Accordingly, option (d), 'inside' is the most appropriate word that denotes the place where the treasure is buried, with respect to the well. 'On' denotes 'to denote still surfaces', 'from' denotes the starting point of a journey or a source, 'of' denotes the relationship between two things/persons and 'at' denotes a particular location and so, these are negated.

t: Identify the sentence in which the word “since” is used as a preposition.
o: Since the roads were flooded, the buses could not operate normally.
I have not spoken to her since Monday.
Since you insist, I will reconsider the proposal.
The company has expanded rapidly since it changed its management.
e: Answer: B) I have not spoken to her since Monday. Explanation: A preposition is followed by a noun or pronoun and shows its relationship with another word. In option B, “since” is followed by the noun “Monday.” since Monday Therefore, “since” functions as a preposition. Why other options are incorrect: A) “since” joins two clauses: Since the roads were flooded + the buses could not operate normally. Hence, it is a conjunction. C) “since” introduces the clause “you insist.” Therefore, it is a conjunction. D) “since” connects two clauses: The company has expanded rapidly + it changed its management. Hence, it is a conjunction.
